title: It Has Happened
label: ch:ml-perfect
canDo: I can say that something has happened and still bears on now, not only that it happened.

payoff.summary: From cold: four shapes off one past form, and the word already in hand that finished the last of them.
payoff.note: THE NOTE WAS HALF STALE AND HALF RIGHT, which is why this point was worth opening carefully rather than trusting either way. 'Neither the participle nor the construction appears' -- the PARTICIPLE half is FALSE: ML-C90-past-participle teaches vanna at sequence 3180, and it even establishes the regularity the Spanish source points ask about (A1-V-10 irregular participles, A1-V-14 the regular one), saying outright that the rule is 'about the letter and not about the tense'. The CONSTRUCTION half is TRUE: a census for -ittu returned ZERO files. SO THE CHAPTER COSTS NO VOCABULARY. Both halves of the perfect were already owned -- the past vannu at ML-C32-varuka, and undu at ML-C32-undu (sequence 650), whose gloss has read '[someone] has' since it was written. What was missing was only the join, and the recall asks the learner outright how many new words the chapter cost. FOUR SHAPES OFF ONE PAST FORM is the chapter's spine: vannu, then vanna (a vowel sign taken OFF, which is ML-C90's own framing), then vannittu (-ittu put ON), then vannittundu. Each row is the row above it with one change, and the contrast between taking away and adding is what makes the new form memorable rather than arbitrary. THE EXAMPLE VERB WAS CHOSEN, NOT DEFAULTED TO. varuka is the verb ML-C90 already uses, so the chapter chains directly off the lesson it extends. pokuka was rejected: its past poyi appears only INSIDE the multi-word headword 'poyi varaam', so it owns no single token and is not independently taught -- the same multi-word trap that narrowed chapter 18's examples. avan IS taught (ML-C71-avan-aval, sequence 2430) and is wired as a dependency. Worth recording separately: ML-A1-F-33's note still claims 'there is no third-person pronoun', which this chapter's checking incidentally disproves.
